name: Marco Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at a mid-size city supermarket, the kind wedged under a block of flats, and I split my week between the tills and picking online orders. Picking means I walk the aisles with a handheld scanner and a trolley of six crates, filling people's shopping before the vans leave at eleven. I like the picking more, because it's a puzzle, beating the route time. The tills on a Saturday afternoon wear me out, the queue never ends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been there, and how are things at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Seven years now, and they pay me a bit above the rest because I can cover the tills, the picking and the kiosk. I live with my partner Inès, who's in her last year of nursing school. I've got about eight months of pay saved and a small index fund I've been feeding since I was twenty-two. I use AI tools every day, for meal plans, sorting bills, even practising Spanish on the bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief for a lot of people, and I'd say the money should go into wages, not more machines. Online I'd post about using the savings to cut hours instead of jobs. At work I'd joke that the scanner still freezes every morning anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's basically nothing. My picking app already tells me the route, and that's the AI bit. If it stays at that level, I keep my job, my bonus and my routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep both roles and keep putting two hundred a month into the index fund. I'd ask my manager for the kiosk training so I'm the go-to person for the tech. That's it really, life goes on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit bored by it, if I'm honest, because I like new stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored? Say more about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd quite like the shop to change a bit, as long as it's fair. A world where nothing moves means I'm picking the same aisles at forty. I'd probably look for change myself, just not because AI forced it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Inès say about this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say good, more nurses still needed, nothing changes for her. Her job was always safer than mine. We'd keep planning a holiday in the spring.

say: I'd say any **savings** from AI should go into wages, not more machines.
I'd joke at work that the **scanner** still freezes every morning anyway.
think: My **picking app** already does the AI bit, so my job barely changes.
If nothing moves, I keep my **bonus**, my routine and my two roles.
do: Keep both roles and put **£200 a month** into the index fund.
Ask my manager for the **kiosk training** to become the go-to tech person.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit bored, because he likes new things.
S0.quote: A world where nothing moves means I'm picking the same aisles at forty.
fieldNote: He is **curious** enough to find a no-change world slightly dull.
His job already includes a **route app**, so modest AI feels familiar.
A partner in **nursing** steadies the household's sense of safety.

steps.text: Keep splitting the week between tills and online picking
Put 200 a month into the index fund
Ask the manager for training on the ordering kiosks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to share out the gains, like a four-day week for shop staff. I'd post about it, and I'd tell the younger lads at work to learn the machines now. I'd be upbeat in public, because I actually think it can go well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully it's good for me. The thinking stuff, the ordering and the rotas, goes to software, and someone has to fix the robots when they come in slowly. That someone could be me, if I move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for an evening course in electrical maintenance this winter, about eight hundred, paid from savings. I'd volunteer to be the store's self-checkout and robot contact. I'd keep feeding the index fund, maybe more, because these firms will grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A bit guilty, because not everyone at the store can do what I'm planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you feel guilty about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Joyce on the bakery counter, who's fifty-eight and hates any screen. She'd be the first one told her role is merged. I'd want the union to make sure she's looked after, not pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're investing in the firms that might cut jobs. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not totally, no. But if robots do the work, I'd rather own a tiny slice of them than nothing. I'd still vote for taxing them properly.

say: I'd push for a **four-day week** for shop staff to share out the gains.
I'd tell younger colleagues to **learn the machines** now, while there's time.
think: The **ordering and rotas** move to software, but someone has to fix robots.
If I **move early**, that repair job could be mine.
do: Take an **electrical maintenance** evening course this winter, about £800 from savings.
Volunteer to be the store's **robot contact** and keep feeding the index fund.
feel: **Excited**, with some guilt for colleagues who can't follow him.
S1.quote: If robots do the work, I'd rather own a tiny slice of them than nothing.
fieldNote: He reads **Steady Disruption** as an opening, not a threat.
Guilt about **older colleagues** sits alongside his own excitement.
He sees no conflict between **investing** in robot firms and taxing them.

steps.text: Pay 800 for an evening electrical maintenance course this winter
Volunteer as the store's self-checkout and robot contact
Vote for parties that would tax robots properly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that we need a robot dividend, now, before 2031. Something like a share of the profits paid to everyone, because nobody can retrain this fast. I'd join every campaign going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the 2028 bit doesn't scare me, because the thinking part of my job is tiny. The 2031 bit does. Picking an online order is a perfect robot job, so robots would take my favourite part of the job first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away I'd do the maintenance course, but faster, a full-time crash course using four months of savings. I'd try to get hired by the firm installing the robots in our chain. I'd keep a big chunk of savings untouched, because I don't know what jobs exist in 2032.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but busy. Being busy keeps the fear down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the robot installers don't need you either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm in trouble like everyone else. Robots fixing robots isn't fantasy in that world. That's the bit I can't plan around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Inès change any plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd hold off on having kids for a while, though we weren't rushing anyway. We'd lean on her wage, because hospitals would still need nurses for a bit longer. It'd flip who carries the household for a while.

say: I'd demand a **robot dividend** before 2031, a share of profits for everyone.
I'd join every **campaign** going, because nobody can retrain this fast.
think: The **2028** part barely touches me, because my thinking work is tiny.
By **2031**, picking robots would take my favourite part of the job first.
do: Do a full-time **maintenance crash course**, spending four months of savings.
Apply to the firm **installing robots** across our chain, keeping the rest saved.
feel: **Anxious** but busy, using action to keep fear down.
S2.quote: Picking an online order is a perfect robot job, so robots would take my favourite part of the job first.
fieldNote: He clearly separates the **2028 thinking wave** from the 2031 robot wave.
His plan relies on **robot installers** still needing people, which he doubts.
The household would lean on **Inès's nursing wage** for a while.

steps.text: Spend four months of savings on a full-time maintenance course
Apply to the firm installing robots across the supermarket chain
Campaign for a robot dividend paid from company profits
Put off having children with Inès for a few years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as the fast one, robot dividend and shorter weeks, but I'd say it with more hope. Five years is enough to set things up if governments get going. I'd be at the meetings, not just online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's tight but workable for me. I'd have until about 2034 on the shop floor, and by then I could be the person maintaining the picking robots. The office side going in 2031 would actually make my store manager need tech people more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the part-time course next year and keep the job. In year two I'd ask to shadow the engineer who services our self-checkouts. I'd keep putting two hundred a month into the fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit nervous, mostly fine. I like having a target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Joyce on the bakery counter in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Joyce she's got a few years, so do the pension sums now. Maybe she can go early with a decent package. I'd help her fill the forms in, she hates those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the worst case for you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The worst case is the robot firms bring their own engineers and never hire locals, and then I'm a trained guy with no door to knock on. I'd still have savings, so I'd be okay for a year at least.

say: I'd keep pushing a **robot dividend** and shorter weeks, but with more hope.
I'd go to the **meetings** in person, not just post online.
think: I'd have until about **2034** on the shop floor, enough to retrain.
When office jobs go in **2031**, my manager would need tech people more.
do: Start a **part-time course** next year while keeping my job.
Ask to **shadow the engineer** who services our self-checkouts in year two.
feel: A bit **nervous**, but mostly fine because he likes a target.
S3.quote: The worst case is the robot firms bring their own engineers and never hire locals, and then I'm a trained guy with no door to knock on.
fieldNote: Five years turns his crash plan into a **steady ladder**.
He worries about **outside engineers** shutting locals out of the new jobs.
He offers practical help to colleague **Joyce**, showing his care for older staff.

steps.text: Start a part-time maintenance course next year
Shadow the engineer who services the self-checkouts
Keep paying 200 a month into the index fund
Attend union meetings pushing for shorter weeks

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and it'd be a scandal to waste it. I'd push for free retraining for every shop worker. At work I'd be the annoying guy talking about it at lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm fine in this one. I'd be thirty-seven when the robots come, with a trade already. I might even run a small team of robot techs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the course properly over two years, then move to the maintenance team. I'd keep the index fund going and maybe help Inès with a deposit on a flat. I'd keep using AI every day to learn the wiring and the fault codes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit hopeful about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a downside you can see?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That a ten-year warning makes people lazy about it. My colleagues would say there's loads of time, and then there's not. I'd keep nagging them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in retail at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but on the tech side. I know shops, and I know what breaks at seven on a Saturday, so that's worth something to a robot firm.

say: I'd call **ten years** a gift and say wasting it would be a scandal.
I'd push for **free retraining** for every shop worker.
think: I'd be **thirty-seven** with a trade when robots arrive, so I'm fine.
I might even run a **small team** of robot technicians.
do: Do the **course** over two years, then move to the maintenance team.
Help Inès toward a **flat deposit** while keeping the index fund going.
S4.quote: I know shops, and I know what breaks at seven on a Saturday, so that's worth something to a robot firm.
fieldNote: A decade lets him plan a **trade**, not a scramble.
His worry turns to colleagues getting **complacent**.
He sees his **shop floor know-how** as an asset, not dead weight.

steps.text: Complete the maintenance course over two years
Move onto the chain's robot maintenance team
Save toward a flat deposit with Inès
Use AI tools daily to learn wiring and fault codes

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even someone like me, who likes this stuff, can't retrain in three years with any certainty. What would help is a robot dividend and paid time off to retrain. Proper rules that the robot firms train local people would help too.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what we'd lose. I'd miss the chat with the delivery drivers at six in the morning. Robots get a lot done, but the shop gets lonelier.

headlineQuote: Robots get a lot done, but the shop gets lonelier.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old** cashier and online-order picker at a city supermarket, seven years in.
He has eight months saved, an **index fund** and a partner, Inès, training as a nurse.
He uses **AI every day** and sees robot maintenance as his next trade.
He stays calm in slow scenarios and becomes **anxious but busy** when AGI arrives fast.
He pairs personal ambition with a strong push for a **robot dividend**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because even keen learners can't retrain with certainty in three years.
whatWouldHelp: A **robot dividend**, paid time off to retrain, and rules that robot firms train local people.
